title: Forming his own trio: Mitchell, Bennett, Simpkins, Budwig, Bailey
summary: His Sunday and Monday trio went through many bass players and drummers, including Frank Butler, until Monty Budwig and Donald Bailey made his best trio.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: There was a club across the street where a guy let me form a Jazz trio, playing two nights a week, Sunday and

Monday. And I got these two guys. First I started with Red Mitchell and Nick Martinez; and then Red got a chance to do something else that was better, and I got Max Bennett -- so I had those two guys for a while. And the trio, we used to work around whenever we could.

Then I switched drummers, and I had a little set-to with Max Bennett, and all of a sudden I was without my trio. But this guy called me down at the Beach, so I got Andy Simpkins and Stix Hooper. And we worked up a tremendous trio. Andy... Well, you know who they are.

So all of a sudden, somebody shows up and brings in George Shearing to listen to this trio, and it just so happened that he was looking for a drummer and a bass -- and there went my bass and drums. And then I'm dead again.

So now I go through about six bass players, and I finally got Monty Budwig. And we were having our problems with the drums. I couldn't depend on Frank Butler, because he'd sell his drums; he was sick, you know, with the needle.
He was one of the best drummers around. It's just too bad. It's a tragedy. And he died... Yeah, he was one of my very, very good friends, and he was a tremendous

drummer.
Well, that job lasted quite a while. I kept switching drummers. I can't remember who I'd find... I finally got Donald Bailey. That was my favorite. He is my favorite drummer, Donald Bailey -- and I got him. And that was the beginning of my trio. Probably the best trio I ever had was Donald Bailey and Monty Budwig. And then I started writing out some real bass parts. I didn't write drum parts in those days. And no piano parts. So nobody could steal the library, because nobody knew what the heck the tunes were. I was writing out all the Wayne Shorter tunes, and all the Jazz tunes I'd hear on the records, you know, from Horace Silver and everybody, you know...
We had a helluva trio. And all the drummers would come around: "Where in the world did you get that drummer." I'd say, "Never mind. I got him. You keep your hands off him. He's my drummer."
